reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A true osteonecrosis of a lesser metatarsal head, most commonly the second, rather than a traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the metatarsal head, with the second metatarsal involved most often, followed by the third
Typically presents in adolescents around puberty and is notable for being more common in girls than boys
Complaints include forefoot pain and swelling localised to the affected metatarsophalangeal joint, worse on weight-bearing and push-off
The radiographic hallmark is flattening, sclerosis and collapse of the metatarsal head with widening of the joint and later osteophytes and loose bodies
The Smillie staging system describes progression from subchondral change to head flattening, fragmentation and joint destruction
It is one of the few osteochondroses that predominates in females, possibly reflecting footwear and loading patterns
Management ranges from offloading with orthoses and activity modification to joint debridement or reconstructive surgery for advanced disease as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Freiberg infraction is an osteonecrosis of the head of a lesser metatarsal, usually the second, resulting from interruption of the subchondral blood supply. Repetitive loading and microtrauma across a relatively long or rigid second metatarsal are thought to produce subchondral stress and vascular compromise, leading to necrosis of the articular bone. The subchondral bone subsequently collapses, the metatarsal head flattens and the articular cartilage fissures and fragments. Progressive incongruity of the metatarsophalangeal joint follows, with loose body formation, osteophytosis and secondary degenerative arthritis. A comparatively long second metatarsal and the increased forefoot loading associated with certain footwear are recognised contributing factors.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis of a metatarsophalangeal joint
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing forefoot radiographs to assess metatarsal head flattening, sclerosis and joint changes
Magnetic resonance imaging for early disease before collapse and to assess the articular surface
Assessment of relative metatarsal lengths and forefoot loading pattern
Smillie staging on radiographs to guide management
Ultrasound to evaluate synovitis or to exclude an interdigital neuroma
Inflammatory markers if septic arthritis is a concern
redFlags: Advanced head collapse with joint destruction and fixed deformity
Locking or mechanical symptoms suggesting intra-articular loose bodies
Warmth, marked swelling or systemic features raising the possibility of infection
Progressive pain despite conservative measures indicating the need for surgical assessment
reference.prognosis: Early disease often responds well to offloading and activity modification, but established head collapse and articular fragmentation may progress to metatarsophalangeal osteoarthritis with persistent pain requiring surgical intervention.
pitfalls: Attributing forefoot pain to a neuroma and overlooking metatarsal head osteonecrosis on radiographs
Missing early disease when plain films are normal and not obtaining magnetic resonance imaging
Failing to address abnormal forefoot loading or footwear as a contributing factor
Delaying surgical referral once joint incongruity and mechanical symptoms have developed
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
